To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

visual attention and visual working (short-term) memory share the same limited capacity resources and that this capacity limitation is a key constraint for the way in which we can cope with the simultaneous demands on visual attentional and working memory processes.
participants are able to encode into visual WM items that are not perceptually distinct from their background but that this requires additional time and effort.

visual selective attention and visual WM share the same capacity limited resources, and that this is reflected in the fact that participants are able to achieve high WM performance in all stimulation condition but, in the conditions that demand a lot of attentional resources, they need more processing time to achieve that high performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between attention and memory.
how people can cope with the limited capacity of visual attention and working memory in everyday life.
understanding how visual working memory is used to cope with real life situations in which the demand for visual attention and visual working memories occur simultaneously.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the findings are in line with the assumption that the memory for location of target objects substitutes for the perceptual pop-out of target objects.
the memory for the target locations substitutes for the perceptual pop-out in the non pop-out condition.
attentional demand influences strategies of encoding into visual WM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human visual system has the ability to flexibly adjust the processing of visual information according to the task demands.
the capacity-limited resources for visual WM are shared with the attention system, but that WM can compensate for the lack of attentional resources by memorizing target locations.
attentional resources are a bottleneck in visual WM and that the bottleneck can be circumvented by a memory for target locations that substitutes for attentional selection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we are able to cope with the common processing limitation of visual attention and WM by using the memory for target location as a substitute for perceptual pop out.

, in situations in which the capacity-limited resources of visual working memory and visual selective attention are simultaneously required, participants are able to compensate for the absence of perceptual pop-out by using the memory for target location as a proxy for pop-out.
the capacity limitations of attention and memory are not necessarily a burden but may actually allow for flexible and adaptive behavior.
